text: Specifically, we suggest that a Duchenne smile is implicitly associated with psychological proximity, whereas a non-Duchenne smile is associated with psychological distance. Construal-level theory (CLT; Liberman and Trope, 2008 ; Trope and Liberman, 2010 ) posits that psychological distance induces abstract (versus concrete) processing of information. Abstract construal levels shift perception focus to general, central, stereotypical aspects and fewer details, whereas concrete construal levels draw attention to individual detail and consideration of peripheral aspects ( Liberman and Trope, 1998 ). Furthermore, abstract construal levels lead to an overgeneralization of perceived social psychological distance as well as other psychological distances such as spatial, temporal, and hypothetical ( Bar-Anan et al., 2006 ; Trope and Liberman, 2010 ). Researchers have related a plethora of perception effects and behavioral consequences to such changes in construal level and psychological distances (for a recent meta-analysis, see Soderberg et al., 2015 ). If different smiles could relate to different psychological distances—and thus construal levels—of an audience, knowledge about this effect provides a tool for communicators to support their intended messages subtly. Our two hypothetical smiling communicators, for example, might use non-Duchenne and Duchenne smiles to bolster their respective messages.
source_label: Proximity Begins with a Smile, But Which One? Associating Non-duchenne Smiles with Higher Psychological Distance
